name: Walking Street, Pattaya
label: Walking Street
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Soi 13/4' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Soi 13/4 nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/31981734: the middle of the OpenStreetMap line 'Pattaya Sai Nueng Road' (766 m long).
notes: Famous neon-lit nightlife street, best photographed at dusk.

text.description:
Walking Street is Pattaya's best-known evening strip: a long, neon-lit road of restaurants, bars, music venues and clubs that fills with people once the sun goes down. It began as a road serving a fishing village. In the 1960s and 70s it changed to cater for visiting American soldiers on leave, and it was closed to traffic in the evening after a run of car accidents in the 1990s. A large video sign went up at the Beach Road entrance in March 2010.

It is near Soi 13/4, a narrow side lane. Please check the exact spot on the day. The lane has bare-bulb string lights overhead, which give warm light and a good backdrop for portraits, and usually fewer people in frame than on the main strip. Most visitors walk straight past it.

For the wide neon scene, two other places work well. One is under the illuminated entrance arch, with the crowd moving beneath it. The other is Bali Hai Pier, where a zoomed view back up the street squeezes the signs together. Keep your phone out of the venues themselves and avoid photographing bar staff. Street performers and animals usually expect a tip if you photograph them. Please confirm the lane on the map before you set off.
text.geographic_location: Walking Street is in Pattaya, a pedestrianised evening strip running from the Beach Road entrance down towards the Bali Hai pier.
text.directions_text: There are no Underground-style stations or tram stops here, so go by taxi or hired scooter from wherever you are staying in Pattaya and ask for the Walking Street entrance arch. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lane and the lights overhead. Switch to 2x for portraits, as it flatters faces and keeps the background softer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want to show the whole line of bulbs stretching above you.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Soi 13/4 (Side alley branching off Walking Street about a third of the way down from the arch). A narrow side lane with overhead bare-bulb string lights, giving warm light and a portrait-friendly backdrop with fewer people in frame. From here the main Walking Street lies to the south-west. Face along the lane with the string lights above and behind your subject, so the bulbs glow in the background.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place your subject on one of the vertical lines, with the strings of bulbs running away behind them. Hold the phone at chest height and tilt up slightly so the lights fill the top of the frame. For the full neon street, try the entrance arch with the crowd passing under it, or a zoomed view from Bali Hai Pier looking back up the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Use portrait mode for people, and tap on your subject's face to focus. Then slide the exposure down a little so the bulbs stay warm and don't burn out. Let night mode do its work and hold still for a couple of seconds. Ask people to stay still as well, because moving figures blur in low light.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: After dark, when the string lights are lit and the street is open to pedestrians. Earlier in the evening the lane is likely to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is an open public street, closed to vehicles in the evening. Check locally for current rules. Tripods are not encouraged, and avoid photographing inside venues or bar staff.

name: Sanctuary of Truth
label: Sanctuary of Truth
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sanctuary of Truth' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223698118: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sanctuary of Truth' (108 m across).
notes: Giant carved all-wood temple on the Naklua coast.

text.description:
The Sanctuary of Truth is a huge temple-like building in Pattaya, carved almost entirely from wood. It is still unfinished: work began in 1981 and carries on today, which is why visitors are given hard hats to wear inside. The grounds cover 13 hectares, and the tallest spire reaches 105 metres. The design draws on the temples of Ayutthaya and on Hindu and Buddhist ideas, so the building is richly decorated with hand-carved wooden figures, gods and ornament.

It photographs well because of the detail and the setting. From the sea-facing waterfront platform at the water's edge you can look back up at the whole structure with open water and coastline behind it, which the front view cannot give you. Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for this angle, and it also suits a walking shot or a photo of two people with the building above them.

If you want a second angle, the View Point of the Sanctuary of Truth gives one wide frame of the wooden façade and spires with the sea behind. For the front of the building, stand further back so the full height fits without the sideways-tilting look you get close up. Go earlier in the day if you want fewer people in the frame. Take a moment to step in close for the carvings too: the wood textures are the real character of the place.
text.geographic_location: In Pattaya, on the coast, where the building stands at the water's edge with the open sea behind it.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot. The sea-side platform is inside the ticketed grounds, so you enter the site first and take your sea-side photos from within it. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) on the waterfront platform when you want the whole structure and the sea in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, more natural view of the building. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carved figures and spire details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The sea-side viewpoint is the waterfront platform at the water's edge, inside the ticketed grounds. From there your photo shows the whole structure rising above you with the open sea and coastline as the backdrop.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the building's vertical lines straight on them. Tilting the phone upwards makes the spires lean inwards, so hold it level and step back if you can. The View Point of the Sanctuary of Truth is a good alternative: it gives one wide frame of the wooden façade and spires with the sea behind. For the front of the building, shoot from a distance so the full height fits without the upward distortion you get up close.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the carved wood. Take a few frames of each view, because other visitors move through the shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for the sea-side view. Early morning is said to be quieter.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed site, and hard hats are required inside, so check the official site before you go for hours, ticket rules and any limits on tripods or drones.

name: Pattaya Beach
label: Pattaya Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pattaya City Sign' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'ป้าย Pattaya City' (node/11210117797): point.
pin_note: Position from OSM W149698464 (Pattaya Beach): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: The main curved city beach along Beach Road.

text.description: Pattaya Beach is the long curve of sand and sea that gives the city its postcard look, and on this map the best way to photograph it is from the Pattaya City Sign. The large lettering sits on the hillside, so you can put the words in the foreground and let the beach and the sea fill the background. That makes a bolder, more graphic picture than a plain beach snap, and it tells everyone looking at it exactly where you were. Photo guides describe the sign as a popular photo spot, with a view over both the city and the sea. For a different take, the hilltop viewpoint on Khao Phra Tamnak gives a wide panorama of the whole bay, with the hotel strip following the shoreline and Koh Larn offshore. Tour groups crowd that hilltop viewpoint, so arrive early there. Down on the sand itself, a low shot of the shoreline works well when the sun sets over the water to the west. Keep your phone steady, clean the lens with your sleeve before you start, and take a few frames with and without people in them. Leave a little space around the lettering so nothing is cut off at the edges.
text.geographic_location: Pattaya Beach is the main city beach in Pattaya, on the curve of the bay beside Beach Road. The City Sign stands on the hillside towards the north end of Beach Road, looking over the city and the sea.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed for this spot, so start from the centre of Pattaya and head for the Pattaya City Sign, towards the north end of Beach Road. No public transport is listed, so a taxi is a sensible option. If you also visit the hilltop viewpoint on Khao Phra Tamnak, the climb is steep, so a taxi is advised there. Ask the driver to wait or arrange your return before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the sign and the bay both fit in the frame. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the lettering and want to keep all of it in. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out details such as boats on the water or Koh Larn offshore.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (north end of Beach Road, on the hillside). The large city lettering in the foreground with the beach and sea behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the lettering along the lower third, with the sea and sky filling the rest. Crouch slightly so the letters rise against the water. If the sign is busy, wait a moment for a gap rather than zooming in. For a different view, the hilltop viewpoint on Khao Phra Tamnak gives a wide bay panorama, and the sand at the beach is good for a low shot at sunset.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sea or the sign to focus, then use the exposure slider to stop the sky from turning white. If the lettering looks dark against a bright background, raise the exposure a little. Panorama mode works well on the hilltop viewpoint if you hold the phone steady and sweep slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Tour groups crowd the hilltop viewpoint, so arriving early is advised there. For the beach shot, late afternoon is best because the sun sets over the water to the west.

text.access_note: The sign is not listed as a paid spot, but access and any opening times can change, so check the official site or local signage before you go.

name: Pattaya Floating Market
label: Floating Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Pattaya Floating Market' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM N6815508922 (Pattaya Floating Market): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Four-region Thai market built over canals.

text.description: Pattaya Floating Market is a canal-side market built on the water, where wooden stilt shops and vendor boats line the banks. It photographs well because everything you want is close together: colourful stalls, timber walkways, bridge railings and boats moving along the canal. The classic picture is taken from water level, from a rowed or motor boat on the main canal. From there you see the vendor boats and stilt shops lining the water, with a paddle boat in the foreground, which gives the familiar floating-market look. The boat ride is the main way to get that angle. The market stands at 451/304 Moo 12, on Sukhumvit Road. Entry is ticketed and boat rides cost extra, so check entry fee and opening hours on arrival. On the walkways you can take a second picture looking along the canal as it recedes between the stilt shops and boats. The bridge railings and wooden buildings help to show depth, and the water adds reflections. Soft light cuts down glare on the water, so late afternoon is a good time to aim for. If you want a close photo of a vendor or their stall, ask first. Tripods are discouraged here, but you will not need one with a phone. Hold it with both hands, especially on the boat.
text.geographic_location: The market is on Sukhumvit Road in Pattaya (451/304 Moo 12).
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot; head for the market on Sukhumvit Road (451/304 Moo 12). Boat rides are available and cost extra. Check entry fee and opening hours on arrival. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the boat-level view of vendor boats and stilt shops. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) from the walkways to take in the canal and the bridge railings. Use telephoto (2x or more) for stall details, with the vendor's permission.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. For the classic shot, sit low in a boat on the main canal at water level. The photo shows vendor boats and stilt shops lining the canal, with a paddle boat in the foreground. This is the angle guides describe as the postcard view of the market.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the phone low, close to the water, with the paddle boat in the foreground and the stilt shops running off along the canal behind it. Turn on gridlines and put the canal on a diagonal or in the centre to give depth. For an alternative, stand on the walkway and shoot along the canal as it recedes, using the bridge railings and wooden buildings as a frame. Wait for a calm patch of water so the reflections look clean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boats or stalls to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so bright sky and water do not wash out. Use ultra-wide for the long canal view. Live Photos can catch a boat moving through the frame. Hold the phone with both hands when you are on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the light is softer.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed site, with boat rides costing extra, so check entry fee and opening hours on arrival.

name: Central Pattaya
label: Central Pattaya
camera_pill: near ซอยพัทยา 9
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/151000011: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Central Pattaya' (354 m across).

text.description:
Central Pattaya is a large shopping mall on the Pattaya seafront. It opened in 2009 and is described as the largest beachfront shopping centre in Southeast Asia. It is a big, busy building, and that is what makes it easy to photograph: the front is gently curved, about 111 metres wide, with a lot of wood and glass, and palm trees line the beach side. A plaza and escalators lead up from the beach. The Hilton Pattaya sits on top of the mall, and the hotel tower is what you notice from far away, so the building works both as a close-up subject and as a landmark along the bay.

The mall has seven floors and more than 370 shops, with a cinema, a bowling alley and food courts, so there is plenty of life around it. For a phone photo, aim for the whole curved front with the palms in the foreground, then take a second shot of the tower rising above the roofline. Keep your phone upright for the tower and sideways for the wide front. Turn on the gridlines so the verticals stay straight, and tap the brightest part of the sky if the glass looks too dark.
text.geographic_location: On Pattaya's beachfront, between Pattaya Beach Road and Pattaya 2nd Road, around Pattaya Beach Soi 9.
text.directions_text: Head for the stretch of Pattaya Beach Road near Pattaya Beach Soi 9, which is where the mall's beach side faces the sea. The phone icon on the map is about 120 m north-west of the numbered pin. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the wide curved front and the palms in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of the entrance and plaza. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Hilton tower and the details of the façade.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 120 m north-west of the numbered pin, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. You will be close to the building, so use the ultra-wide lens for the full front.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the vertical edges of the building up with them. Put the palm trees along one side as a frame, and leave some sky above so the tower is not cut off. Take one wide shot of the whole front and one tighter shot of the tower.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the building and drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky keeps its colour. After dark, use night mode and hold the phone against something steady, or brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon gives softer light on the front, and after dark the lit building works well in night mode.

text.access_note: The mall is a public shopping centre; check the official site before you go for opening times and any rules about photography inside.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon light is softer on the building.
The building looks good lit up after dark and suits night mode.
The beach side of the mall faces the sea along Pattaya Beach Road.

name: Bali Hai Pier
label: Bali Hai Pier
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bali Hai Pier' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OSM W754202333 (Pattaya Bali Hai Pier): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Pier at the end of Walking Street with ferries to Koh Larn.

text.description:
Bali Hai Pier is a working pier on the Pattaya waterfront, with ferries and anchored boats in front of the open bay. That mix of boats, water and sky gives you a lively scene that is easy to photograph without any special planning. From the outer end of the pier you look back across the bay, and the curve of Pattaya Beach sweeps away to the north behind the boats. That makes it a good place for a wide, scene-setting shot of the town from the water.

Walk to the far end of the pier for the open view. The boats close to you fill the foreground, and the bay and the beach curve fill the background. Keep the horizon level, and use the boats as a leading line towards the beach. If you want a different angle, the viewpoints at Khao Phra Tamnak (a high view down onto the pier, bay and city) and Laem Bali Hai (the lighthouse with the pier and boats beyond it) show the same scene from other positions. Which one suits you depends on how much walking you want to do.

The ferry loading areas can get busy, so stay clear of the gangways when boats are docking. Late afternoon, roughly 5:00 to 6:30 PM, brings golden light, and early morning is also good for softer light.
text.geographic_location: Bali Hai Pier is on the Pattaya waterfront, with the long curve of Pattaya Beach to the north. Khao Phra Tamnak and Laem Bali Hai are also recommended viewpoints for this scene.
text.directions_text: Head for the Bali Hai Pier area on the waterfront. No nearby Underground, tram or train stops are listed, so head for Bali Hai Pier itself to find your way. Once you are on the pier, walk to the outer end, where the phone icon on the map is. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole bay, boats and beach curve in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single ferry or the far end of the beach.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From there you see ferries and anchored boats in the foreground, with the bay and the curve of Pattaya Beach to the north behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on a line, then keep a boat or two in the lower part of the frame and the beach curve across the middle. Crouching a little gives more water and sky. If you want a high view of the pier, try Khao Phra Tamnak. For the lighthouse with the pier behind it, try Laem Bali Hai.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the boats to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch so the sky keeps its colour. Wipe the lens first, as sea air leaves a haze on it. A Live Photo can catch boats moving on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 5:00 to 6:30 PM, for golden light. Early morning is also good for soft light.

text.access_note: The pier is a public waterfront space and a ferry departure point, so keep clear of the ferry loading areas and gangways when boats are docking.

name: Mini Siam

pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4623282095: the OpenStreetMap point 'mini Siam'.

text.description: Mini Siam is a miniature park in Pattaya where famous buildings are rebuilt at a scale of 1:25. That makes it a good place for a phone camera: the models are small enough to fill the frame, and the gardens around them help them look like the real thing. The Thai section has replicas of well-known temples, and the best view is at its entrance, looking towards the models of the Emerald Buddha temple and Wat Arun, with the park's gardens behind. The park's founder, Kasem Kasemkietsakul, wanted to bring famous landmarks together in one place so visitors could learn about architecture. The first model built was the Democracy Monument from Bangkok. A small stretch of water divides the Thai section from the Mini Europe section. In Mini Europe, the Sydney Opera House replica sits against that water, which makes a second good photo if you have time. Stand at the entrance of the Thai section, hold your phone at about eye level and keep the temples in the middle of the picture, with garden around them. Keep to the paths and don't step into the replica areas. Drones are not permitted. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer people in your shot.
text.geographic_location: Mini Siam stands on Sukhumvit Road in Pattaya, Chonburi province, about 143 km from Bangkok.
text.directions_text: Mini Siam is on Sukhumvit Road in Pattaya; check a map app for the route. Once inside the park, walk to the entrance of the Thai section, where the temple models begin. The phone icon on the map is right at the subject, so there is no extra walk once you are there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the temple models and the gardens behind them. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a single temple, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for roof and spire details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see replicas such as the Emerald Buddha temple and Wat Arun, with the park's gardens behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Hold the phone at eye level, turn on gridlines and keep the temple spires upright against them. Let some garden show behind the models. If you have time, try the Sydney Opera House replica in Mini Europe, reflected in the waterway that divides the two sections.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the temple to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so the roofs keep their colour. Try portrait mode on a single model for a softer background.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and the park is quieter.

text.access_note: Mini Siam is a ticketed park, so check the official site for entry details and opening times before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone at eye level and keeping the models in the middle of the frame makes the replicas look more like real buildings.
Lowering the exposure slider can keep roof colours from washing out when the sky is bright.

name: Wong Amat Beach
label: Wong Amat Beach
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Soi Naklua 18' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Soi Naklua 18 nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q106818525: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Cleaner northern beach lined with high-rises.

text.description: Wong Amat Beach is a calm stretch of sand on the Nakluea Bay peninsula in northern Pattaya. It is about 1.3 km long, and unlike Pattaya Beach there is no beach road running beside it, so the view feels more open and relaxed. The scene here is about the shoreline: low rocks, fishing boats, and a wide horizon over the bay. Behind the sand, the luxury condominium towers that went up in the 2010s make a modern backdrop, and the area also has several hotels. The first hotel on this beach opened in 1960, and the beach is named after its original owner, Boonwong Amatayakul. Guides also recommend walking down Soi Naklua 18 to the beach, then heading towards the left-hand rocky end. The low rocks make good foreground shapes against the water, and the open horizon suits sunset and silhouette shots. This end is also said to be quieter than the central part of the beach. If you want a different view, Pattaya Viewpoint shows the whole bay as a wide panorama. Wong Amat appears there as part of the bigger scene rather than as a close subject. Parking is very limited near the beach end.
text.geographic_location: Wong Amat Beach is in the Na Kluea area of northern Pattaya, on the Nakluea Bay peninsula, in Chonburi Province. Guides point visitors down Soi Naklua 18 to the rocky end of the beach.
text.directions_text: No station or stop is listed nearby, so head for Na Kluea in northern Pattaya and Soi Naklua 18. Guides suggest walking down the soi to the beach and turning towards the left-hand rocky end. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for sunset and silhouette shots of the rocks and horizon. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the curve of the shoreline. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a fishing boat on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Soi Naklua 18 (walk down the soi to the beach, then head toward the left-hand rocky end of the beach). Low rocks and an open horizon over the bay, suited to sunset and silhouette shots of the shoreline.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, keeping it level. Place a dark rock or two in the bottom corner as a foreground. If you want a change, Pattaya Viewpoint gives a wide panorama of the bay, where Wong Amat is only part of the scene.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: For a silhouette, tap the bright part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down until the colours look rich and the rocks go dark. Wipe your lens first, as sea air can leave a haze on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset, roughly 17:30 to 18:30 according to one guide. Another guide suggests mornings for quieter light.

text.access_note: The beach is open to walk along, but parking is very limited near the beach end and some shore areas may mean passing through resort grounds, so stay on public paths and check the official site of any hotel before you go.

text.description: Pattaya Park Tower is a tall landmark on the Jomtien side of Pattaya, and it is easiest to photograph from a distance, where you can see how it stands over the surrounding district. This spot does that from the observation platform next to the Big Buddha Temple on Phratamnak Hill. A guide to Pattaya viewpoints describes this platform as one of the few ground-level places where the tower appears in a wide view of the district, and the platform is free to use. Expect a small tower in a big scene rather than a close-up. That suits a phone: take one wide frame that shows the whole setting, then a second, tighter frame to pick out the tower itself. If you would like a different angle, Thappraya Road has a wide panorama of the northern Jomtien shoreline, taken from the beach near the corner, with the tower in the frame. We have not been able to confirm the exact framing from either place, so take a few test shots and adjust. The tower is also known for its viewing deck, but that is inside the building and is not a place to photograph it from.
text.geographic_location: On Phratamnak Hill in the south of Pattaya, next to the Big Buddha Temple, looking south-west over Jomtien towards the tower.
text.directions_text: There are no rail or tram stops nearby, so make your own way to the Big Buddha Temple on Phratamnak Hill, and walk to the observation platform beside it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the wide view over Jomtien and Thappraya Street. Then switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the distant tower closer. The ultra-wide (0.5x) makes the tower very small, so use it only if the foreground is interesting.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Big Buddha Temple (observation platform next to the temple, on Phratamnak Hill). An elevated view over Jomtien district and Thappraya Street with Pattaya Park Tower visible in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn to face south-west and switch on the gridlines. Put the tower on one of the vertical lines and keep the streets and rooftops below it, so the tower is clearly part of the district. Keep the horizon level. Take one wide shot and one zoomed shot. If you also visit Thappraya Road, the beach near the corner works well for a panorama with the tower in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tower to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour. With telephoto, hold the phone with both hands and rest your elbows on the rail if it is safe to do so. Use panorama mode for the Thappraya Road alternative and move slowly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a clear day, as haze can wash out a distant tower. Morning or later in the day, when the air is cooler and the light is softer, is usually kinder to the colours than midday.

text.access_note: The platform next to the temple is shown as free to use, but it sits beside a place of worship, so dress respectfully.
claims_not_in_sources: Pattaya Park Tower is on the Jomtien side of Pattaya and has a viewing deck inside the building.
Haze can reduce the clarity of a distant subject on some days.
Morning or later-day light is usually softer than midday light.
The temple is a place of worship where respectful dress is expected.
Pairing the platform with a sunset or morning shot depends on the weather and season.

text.description: Jomtien Beach is the long, curving beach south of central Pattaya, on the Gulf of Thailand. It is lined with high-rise condominiums, beachside hotels and restaurants, and runs alongside a promenade and the beach road. The beach is popular for swimming and windsurfing, and jet skis and parasailing are also on offer, so there is nearly always something going on in the frame. It faces west, which makes it a good place for sunset: the sky colours over the water and kitesurfers sometimes appear in silhouette. The long promenade gives you plenty of angles along the bay, so you can walk a little and try a few. Jomtien is about 3 km south of Pattaya and roughly 165 km south-east of Bangkok. For a first shot, stand on the sand near the promenade, face the gulf and keep the horizon level using your phone's gridlines. Then add a foreground, such as footprints, a beach chair or a passer-by, to give the picture some depth. If you have time, a second view is worth a look: Jomtien Heads Viewpoint gives a wide view south over the curve of the coast, with Koh Larn beyond. Khao Phra Tamnak gives a high view over Pattaya Bay and the beaches below. The routes to both are easiest to check on the map before you set off.
text.geographic_location: Jomtien Beach is in Jomtien, in Bang Lamung District, Chonburi Province, about 3 km south of Pattaya. The beach runs along Jomtien Beach Road, with Second Road about 400 metres inland.
text.directions_text: Start from central Pattaya and head about 3 km south towards Jomtien, by taxi, motorbike taxi or songthaew. Blue songthaews also run between Pattaya and Jomtien Beach. Ask to be dropped on Jomtien Beach Road, then walk onto the sand near the promenade and face the gulf (west) to reach the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the main sunset shot. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for the sweep of the bay and the promenade. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out kitesurfers or a single boat on the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stand on Jomtien Beach, on the sand near the beachfront promenade, and face the gulf.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the horizon on the lower or upper third line, depending on whether the sky or the water is the more interesting part. Include a foreground, such as sand, a railing or a person walking, to give depth. If kitesurfers are out, wait for one to cross the brightest part of the sky. For a different view, Jomtien Heads Viewpoint gives a wide look south over the curving coastline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest part of the sky to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the colours stay rich and the sun does not wash out. For people against the sky, tap on them first and lift the exposure slightly. Try Live Photos for moving waves and kites, and clean the lens, since sea air can leave a film on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon up to sunset. About 5:30-6:30 PM is a typical window, but it shifts with the season, so check the sunset time for your date.

text.access_note: This is an open public beach and promenade, with no entry charge expected; check on arrival if you are unsure, and check the route to the other viewpoints on the map before going.
claims_not_in_sources: Dragging the exposure slider down slightly keeps sky colours richer at sunset.
Sea air can leave a film on a phone lens, so wiping it helps.
Placing the horizon on a gridline third gives a balanced picture.
